newsitem.title: UK: Swoop on alleged war criminals a start-UK minister.
newsitem.headline: Swoop on alleged war criminals a start-UK minister.

text.p: Thursday's dramatic swoop on two alleged war criminals in Bosnia by British special forces signalled stronger international determination to bring such people to trial, Britain said on Sunday.

"This was a signal. This was a start. These people have got to face justice, and we are determined internationally that they are going do to so," Defence Secretary George Robertson said in a BBC television interview.

British troops in the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia shot dead Simo Drljaca, former police chief in the town of Prijedor, on Thursday after he tried to avoid arrest by firing on them.
One soldier suffered a leg wound.

The troops also arrested the director of Prijedor hospital, Milan Kovacevic, wanted for complicity in genocide against Bosnian Moslems and Croats during the war. Kovacevic is now jailed in The Hague awaiting trial.

Robertson said the Prijedor episode reflected an increasing impatience among the 34 nations involved in SFOR at the failure of Bosnian state authorities to live up to their undertakings in the Dayton peace treaty.

"They said they would do certain things, they are simply not doing them. And one of the things they are not doing is bringing to book those who have been accused in the International Court (of Justice at The Hague) of these terrible crimes."
In this context, he said, the Prijedor raids were "an important signal of the resolution not just of this government but of the world community in general".

He pointed to the arrest two weeks ago of the former rebel Serb mayor of Vukovar, Slavko Dokmanovic, for the alleged massacre of 260 Croat hospital patients as another sign that the world community was getting tough.
"I think that not just in Britain but elsewhere there is an increasing determination (to arrest those indicted on war crimes charges)," Robertson said.
He declined to speculate on further operations by SFOR troops against those indicted by the International Criminal Tribunal on ex-Yugoslavia, based in The Hague.
There are 67 people on the public indictment list, the majority of them Serbs including their former wartime president, Radovan Karadzic, and army commander, General Ratko Mladic.
But asked about reports that Karadzic had forsaken his Pale headquarters outside Sarajevo and fled to the neighbouring republic of Montenegro, Robertson said:
"This (the Prijedor incident) will have upset a lot of people who thought they were getting away with it."
"What has happened this week is going to make them less easy in their beds and some of them will do rash things, which may well have further consequences."
